title: THE SERPENT WON THE FIRST CONVERSATION—BUT HE WILL LOSE THE FINAL WAR
paragraphs: THE SERPENT WON THE FIRST CONVERSATION—BUT HE WILL LOSE THE FINAL WAR

The Bible begins with humanity listening to a lie and ends with the devil thrown into the lake of fire. Between those two moments stands a bloodstained cross, an empty tomb, and a Savior who came to reclaim what sin had destroyed. And somewhere inside that story is yours.
There is something terrifying about the first recorded conversation between humanity and the serpent.
Nobody was holding a weapon.
Nobody was screaming.
There was no battlefield. No army marching. No thunder announcing that the greatest spiritual catastrophe in human history was about to unfold.
There was only a garden.
A woman.
A serpent.
And a question.
“Did God really say…?”
That was how the deception began.
Not with an obvious declaration of war against heaven, but with a carefully planted doubt about the goodness and truthfulness of God.

And thousands of years later, that same ancient question still finds its way into hospital rooms, broken marriages, secret addictions, exhausted minds, and hearts that have quietly begun wondering whether obedience to God is worth the cost.
Did God really say He would never leave you?
Did God really say you must forgive?
Did God really say holiness matters?
Did God really say there is hope for someone who has fallen as many times as you have?
Before you answer, understand something.
The serpent who deceived humanity in Genesis is the same enemy whose final defeat is revealed in Revelation.
And the astonishing message of Scripture is not merely that evil will eventually be punished.

It is that Jesus Christ entered the very world corrupted by that ancient deception, carried the consequences of human sin to the cross, rose victorious from the grave, and will bring the devil's rebellion to its appointed end.
The Bible does not begin with Satan as king.
And it certainly does not end with him on the throne.
It begins with God creating a world He declares good.
And it ends with God dwelling forever with His redeemed people.
But between those two beautiful realities lies the story of a rebellion that shattered human innocence, a promise that refused to die, and a Redeemer whose victory changes everything.
And here is the part that should make you keep reading.
The first humans hid from God after listening to the serpent. At the end of Scripture, redeemed humanity sees God's face.
What happened between those two moments?
Everything.
In Genesis 3:1, the serpent approaches Eve with words that challenge God's command.
The original Hebrew describes him as עָרוּם (ʿārûm), meaning crafty, shrewd, or cunning.
This is significant because Genesis 2:25 has just described the man and woman as עֲרוּמִּים (ʿărummîm), naked and without shame.
The Hebrew words are related in sound, creating a striking literary contrast.
Humanity was naked and unashamed.
The serpent was cunning and deceptive.
They possessed innocence.
He employed manipulation.
And the tragedy unfolded when human beings began trusting the creature's interpretation of reality over the Creator's word.
Listen carefully to the serpent's promise in Genesis 3:5.
He suggested that eating the forbidden fruit would open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil.
It was a temptation wrapped around something desirable.
Wisdom.
Freedom.
Elevation.
The possibility of becoming more than they were.
But it invited them to pursue those things through disobedience.
And isn't that how so many destructive decisions still begin?
Nobody wakes up hoping to destroy their family.
Nobody dreams of becoming enslaved to pornography, bitterness, dishonesty, or greed.
Nobody plans to become spiritually numb.
It often begins with a whisper.
Just this once.
You deserve this.
Nobody will know.
God understands.
You can repent later.
And sometimes the most dangerous lie is not that God does not exist.
It is that you can safely live as though His word does not matter.
Eve took the fruit and ate. She gave some to Adam, who was with her, and he ate.
The text does not portray Adam as an innocent bystander. Both participated in the disobedience, and both were accountable before God.
Then something happened that the serpent had not presented honestly.
Their eyes were opened.
But instead of the promised glory, they discovered shame.
Instead of freedom, they experienced fear.
Instead of running toward God, they hid from Him.
Genesis 3:8 describes the man and his wife hiding among the trees of the garden from the presence of the LORD God.
Pause there.
The God whose presence had been their blessing was now the One they feared to face.
Sin had changed their relationship with Him.
And perhaps this is where the ancient story becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it means to hide.
You still attend church.
You still know the worship songs.
You still say “God bless you” when someone asks how you are.
But there are parts of your life you have carefully kept behind closed doors.
The secret habit.
The unresolved hatred.
The private messages.
The compromise nobody knows about.
The prayer life that has almost disappeared.
The smile that convinces everyone you are fine when your soul is barely holding together.
You have learned how to look spiritually alive while feeling painfully distant from God.
And when Scripture is preached, sometimes you do not feel comfort.
You feel exposed.
Adam and Eve tried to cover themselves with fig leaves.
Humanity has been manufacturing fig leaves ever since.
Religion without repentance.
Good deeds without surrender.
Public worship without private obedience.
Excuses that sound reasonable until we stand before the holiness of God.
But there is something remarkable about what happens next.
God calls to the man.
“Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9).
God was not searching because He lacked knowledge.
The question confronted Adam with the reality of his condition.
The sinner had hidden.
And God called him to account.
There is judgment in that encounter, certainly.
But there is also something that should stop every despairing reader in their tracks.
The fall of humanity did not silence the voice of God.
The Lord confronted the sin.
He exposed the excuses.
He pronounced the consequences.
But He also spoke a promise that would reach far beyond Eden.
Genesis 3:15 is often called the protoevangelium, a Latin theological term meaning the first announcement of the gospel.
God addresses the serpent and declares that there will be enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring.
The crucial Hebrew wording includes:
הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ וְאַתָּה תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ עָקֵב
Hûʾ yəšûp̄ḵā rōʾš, wəʾattā təšûp̄ennû ʿāqēḇ.
A close translation is:
“He shall strike your head, and you shall strike his heel.”
The Hebrew verb shuph can convey striking or bruising. The distinction between head and heel is central to the imagery.
A wound to the heel.
A blow to the head.
Genesis does not yet reveal every detail of how this conflict will unfold. Its immediate context concerns hostility between the serpent and the woman's offspring.
But Christians have long understood this passage, in the light of the completed Scriptures, as anticipating the ultimate victory of Jesus Christ over the devil.
The promise was spoken in the very chapter where humanity fell.
Think about that.
Before Abraham was called.
Before Moses stood before Pharaoh.
Before David received the promise of a royal descendant.
Before Bethlehem had a manger.
Before Roman soldiers carried out a crucifixion outside Jerusalem.
God had already announced that the serpent would not have the final word.
The enemy had succeeded in drawing humanity into disobedience.
But he had not overthrown the sovereign purposes of God.
And from that moment forward, Scripture unfolds a history of promise, covenant, judgment, mercy, sacrifice, and redemption that finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The story does not move in a straight line from human improvement to human perfection.
It moves through repeated demonstrations of how desperately humanity needs a Savior.
Cain kills Abel.
The earth becomes filled with violence.
Israel repeatedly turns toward idols.
Kings abuse power.
Prophets are rejected.
Nations rise and fall.
Even the most celebrated biblical figures reveal profound weaknesses.
Noah needed grace.
Abraham needed faith.
Moses needed mercy.
David needed forgiveness.
Peter needed restoration.
And every one of us needs more than religious advice.
We need redemption.
This is why the arrival of Jesus Christ is not merely the introduction of another moral teacher into human history.
It is the arrival of the promised Redeemer.
The eternal Son of God took on true humanity.
John 1:14 declares:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
The Greek word sarx means flesh, emphasizing the reality of His human incarnation.
The One through whom all things were made entered the creation that human sin had corrupted.
Not as a sinner.
Not as another fallen son of Adam.
But as the holy Son of God, fully divine and truly human, who came to save sinners.
And where Adam disobeyed, Jesus obeyed.
Where the first humans yielded to temptation, Christ resisted the tempter.
In Matthew 4, the devil approaches Jesus in the wilderness.
Once again, temptation involves questioning and distorting God's word.
Once again, the issue is whether God's word will be trusted.
But this time the response is different.
Jesus answers with Scripture.
“It is written.”
He does not negotiate with the lie.
He does not surrender His obedience.
He does not treat the Father's word as something to be revised for personal advantage.
The devil departs after failing to turn Him from obedience.
And yet the conflict is far from over.
Jesus continues His ministry.
He heals the sick.
He delivers people from demonic oppression.
He forgives sins.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He exposes religious hypocrisy.
He announces the kingdom of God.
And everywhere He goes, the darkness encounters an authority it cannot command.
In Luke 11:20, Jesus explains that His casting out demons by the finger of God demonstrates that God's kingdom has come upon His hearers.
The arrival of Christ is the arrival of the stronger One.
The serpent's kingdom is being challenged by the rightful King.
But then comes the moment that appears, from a merely human perspective, to be the greatest scandal of all.
The Messiah is betrayed.
Arrested.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
Condemned.
And nailed to a Roman cross.
Imagine being one of His disciples.
You left your former life to follow Him.
You watched Him calm storms.
You saw blind eyes opened.
You heard Him speak with an authority unlike anyone else.
You believed He was the Christ.
And now His body hangs on a cross.
His enemies mock Him.
His followers scatter.
His mother stands in grief.
The One who raised Lazarus from the dead is dying.
How could this possibly be victory?
How could the promised serpent-crusher be hanging helplessly before the world?
How could the Son of God be treated like a criminal?
Here is where the gospel becomes more astonishing than any human story could have invented.
The cross was not the failure of God's plan. It was central to its fulfillment.
Jesus was not dragged into an unforeseen defeat.
He willingly gave His life.
He had already told His disciples that He would suffer, be killed, and rise again.
And in John 10:18, He explains that no one takes His life from Him, but that He lays it down of His own accord.
The crucifixion was a real act of human wickedness.
The suffering was real.
The injustice was real.
The blood was real.
But God was accomplishing redemption through the sacrifice of His Son.
Colossians 2:13–15 describes how God forgives believers' trespasses, cancels the record of debt standing against them, and triumphs over the hostile spiritual powers through Christ.
The Greek text of Colossians 2:15 includes the phrase:
θριαμβεύσας αὐτοὺς ἐν αὐτῷ
thriambeusas autous en autō.

The language speaks of triumphing over them. The final phrase is translated in different ways, commonly understood as triumphing over them in or through Christ or the cross, depending on how the context is interpreted.
The central truth is unmistakable.
The powers that seemed victorious at Calvary were not ultimately victorious.
Christ's sacrificial death accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He bore our sins.
He satisfied the demands of divine justice.
He reconciles believers to God.
And He broke the claim that condemnation held over those who belong to Him.
Hebrews 2:14–15 explains that through death Jesus acted to destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and to deliver those enslaved by the fear of death.
The word translated “destroy” in that passage is related to the Greek verb katargeō, which can mean to render powerless, nullify, or bring to nothing.
It does not mean that Satan immediately ceased to exist at the crucifixion.
Scripture plainly teaches that the devil remains active and that believers must resist him (1 Peter 5:8–9).
Rather, Christ's death decisively undermined the devil's power over those redeemed by Christ, and His final judgment is certain.
That distinction matters.
Because biblical hope is not built on pretending that evil has already disappeared from the world.
It is built on the finished saving work of Jesus and the certainty of His coming victory.
And then came the third day.
The tomb was empty.
The crucified Savior had risen.
Death could not hold Him.
The resurrection was not merely an emotional symbol of hope.
It was God's decisive vindication of His Son and the historical foundation of the Christian proclamation.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:17 that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and believers remain in their sins.
Christianity stands or falls with the reality of the resurrection.
But Christ has been raised, Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:20, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
And now consider the contrast.
In Eden, the serpent led humanity toward death.
At the empty tomb, Jesus emerged victorious over death.
In Eden, humanity's disobedience brought condemnation.
In Christ, grace brings justification and life to those who receive Him by faith.
Romans 5:19 says that through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, and through the obedience of the One many will be made righteous.
Adam and Christ are not equals.
Adam is the representative of fallen humanity.
Christ is the righteous Redeemer who accomplishes what Adam could not.
The first Adam brought ruin through disobedience.
The last Adam, as Paul calls Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:45, brings life through His saving work.
And if you have ever wondered whether your past is too dark for Jesus to redeem, consider what the gospel actually announces.
It does not say you are innocent.
It does not say your sin was harmless.
It does not say repentance is unnecessary.
It says the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse sinners who turn to Him in faith.
It says forgiveness is possible because the Savior paid a price we could never pay.
It says the worst chapter of your life does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
Not because sin is small.
But because Christ is mighty to save.
Perhaps you have betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps your marriage is suffering because of choices you made.
Perhaps your children have seen a version of you that you deeply regret.
Perhaps you have spent years carrying shame over something that happened in secret.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that God has already given up on you.
Do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit exposes sin to lead us toward truth, repentance, and Christ.
The enemy would rather see you remain trapped in accusation, despair, and unbelief.
Revelation 12:10 describes the devil as the accuser of God's people, who accuses them before God day and night.
The Greek word used for “accuser” is κατήγωρ (katēgōr).
It refers to one who brings accusations.
And that description captures something painfully familiar about the experience of shame.
You failed again.
You are a hypocrite.
You will never change.
God could never use someone like you.
Some accusations expose real sins that must be confessed and forsaken.
But the gospel refuses the conclusion that a repentant sinner is beyond the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because their past has been rewritten into innocence.
But because their guilt has been answered by the saving work of Christ.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue in darkness.
But power and mercy to come into the light.
And if this is touching a part of your life that you have been afraid to confront, do not rush past it.
You do not need to expose private details publicly.
But you can stop pretending that you are beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Not as a formula that earns forgiveness.
Not as proof of salvation.
But as an honest expression of a heart that longs to walk in the light.
And if you are not ready to comment, you can still pray sincerely where you are.
God is not waiting for a social media response before He hears a repentant heart.
Now return to the great storyline of Scripture.
Genesis opens with the serpent's deception.
Revelation reveals the final judgment of the deceiver.
In Revelation 12:9, John identifies the dragon as “that ancient serpent,” the one called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.
The Greek expression is:
ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος
ho ophis ho archaios.
“The ancient serpent.”
This is one of the clearest canonical connections between the serpent imagery of Genesis and the devil described in Revelation.
The enemy who appeared in the garden is identified in the final book of Scripture as the ancient serpent.
The deceiver is unmasked.
The rebellion is exposed.
And his end is revealed.
Revelation 20:10 describes the devil being thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where he is tormented forever and ever.
This is not a picture of Satan reigning over hell as an independent monarch.
It is a picture of divine judgment.
Satan is not God's equal.
He is not an eternal rival possessing power comparable to the Creator.
He is a creature in rebellion against the sovereign Lord.
His judgment is not uncertain.
His ultimate defeat is not negotiable.
And the Bible does not end by inviting believers to become fascinated with the devil.
It directs their attention to the victory of God and the Lamb.
Because the most beautiful part of Revelation is not the destruction of the serpent.
It is what follows.
A new heaven.
A new earth.
The holy city.
God dwelling with His people.
Tears wiped away.
Death abolished.
Mourning, crying, and pain brought to an end.
And then, in Revelation 22, the tree of life appears again.
Do you see what God is showing us?
In Genesis 3, humanity is driven from the garden and barred from the tree of life.
In Revelation 22, the tree of life stands within the renewed creation, and God's servants have access to His presence.
The curse is removed.
The throne of God and of the Lamb is there.
And Revelation 22:4 contains one of the most breathtaking promises in all of Scripture:
“They will see his face.”
Think about the distance between those words and the trembling voices of Adam and Eve hiding among the trees.
In Eden, fallen humanity hid from the presence of God.
In the new creation, God's redeemed servants see His face.
In Eden, shame entered.
In the new creation, the curse is gone.
In Eden, death became humanity's terrible reality.
In the new creation, death is no more.
In Eden, the serpent deceived.
In Revelation, the ancient serpent is judged.
And at the center of that entire movement stands Jesus Christ.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Savior who rose.
The King who reigns.
The Lord who is coming again.
The Bible begins with a lost paradise. It ends with a greater hope: redeemed humanity dwelling with God forever through Jesus Christ.
But there is a question that must not be avoided.
Where do you stand in this story?
Because knowing that Satan will be defeated is not the same as belonging to Christ.
Knowing Bible prophecy is not the same as being reconciled to God.
Being familiar with Christian language is not the same as repentance and faith.
You can admire the beauty of the gospel and still resist its call.
You can share Scripture online while privately refusing to surrender to the Lord who inspired it.
You can be deeply interested in the defeat of the devil while remaining unwilling to confront the sin in your own life.
Jesus did not come merely to make us informed spectators of a spiritual conflict.
He came to save sinners and call them to follow Him.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus announces:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
The word metanoeite calls for repentance, a change of mind and heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
The word pisteuete calls for belief or trust.
This is not a call to earn salvation through perfect behavior.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works.
But the grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
Ephesians 2:10 goes on to describe believers as created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Real faith does not purchase salvation through obedience.
Real faith receives Christ and bears fruit through a transformed life.
And that means the invitation today is not simply to feel moved by an article.
It is to come to Jesus.
To confess what you have hidden.
To turn from what is destroying you.
To stop defending the sin that Christ died to forgive.
To trust His mercy more than your excuses.
To follow Him even when obedience costs you something.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps you feel nothing at all, but you know you have been spiritually drifting.
Perhaps you once loved Jesus deeply, but compromise has slowly hardened your heart.
Perhaps you are not yet a believer, and you are beginning to understand that Christianity is not simply about becoming a nicer person.
It is about being reconciled to the living God through the crucified and risen Christ.
Wherever you are, the invitation of the gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
He receives those who come to Him in faith.
John 6:37 records His promise that whoever comes to Him, He will never cast out.
You do not need to make yourself worthy before coming.
You come because you are needy.
You come because He is merciful.
You come because there is no other Savior.
And if you do not know what to say, you can begin with a prayer like this:

“Lord Jesus Christ, I have sinned against You. I have believed lies, followed my own desires, and tried to hide what You already see. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn from sin and trust You. Change my heart, lead me in Your truth, and help me follow You faithfully. You are my only hope. Amen.”
Those words are not magic.
A prayer does not save because it has been repeated.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
But sincere prayer is a fitting response to the gospel, and a repentant heart need not fear approaching the throne of grace.
And please hear this.
If you have fallen, do not make peace with your chains.
If you are weary, do not confuse exhaustion with abandonment.
If you are ashamed, do not allow shame to become your hiding place.
If you are grieving, do not assume your tears mean God has forgotten you.
The serpent's first recorded strategy was to distort the word of God.
One of the believer's great responsibilities is to return to that word, understand it faithfully, and hold fast to Christ.
That is why spiritual growth matters.
A person cannot survive on an occasional emotional moment alone.
We need Scripture when our feelings become unreliable.
We need prayer when temptation is strong.
We need the fellowship of believers when isolation becomes dangerous.
We need sound teaching when attractive falsehoods begin sounding like truth.
We need the ordinary, lifelong work of discipleship.
And this is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to make a personality famous.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn the gospel into a product.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in understanding, and keep their eyes fixed on Jesus Christ.
There are people who will never walk into a church building simply because someone invited them.
But they may read an article shared by a relative.
A grieving mother may find a passage of Scripture in her Facebook feed.
A young man struggling with secret sin may encounter a call to repentance.
A discouraged believer may be reminded of the promises of Christ.
An unbeliever may begin asking questions about the gospel for the first time.
We cannot promise what God will do through any particular post.
But we can faithfully make His word available and pray that He uses it.
Not because sharing a post makes you righteous.
Not because the number of shares measures your love for God.
But because someone within your circle may need to hear the message of Christ.
Send it privately to someone who is searching for answers.
There may come a night when temptation feels louder than truth, when shame returns, or when fear tries to convince you that darkness is winning.
Return to these passages.
Read Genesis 3.
Read Romans 5.
Read Colossians 2.
Read Hebrews 2.
Read Revelation 20–22.
Let the actual words of Scripture, rather than the intensity of an emotional moment, anchor your confidence in Jesus.
If you have experienced the Lord's forgiveness, you are welcome to share a brief testimony.
You do not owe the internet the details of your wounds. Your dignity matters, and your story belongs to you.
But sometimes a sincere word of testimony becomes an encouragement to someone who thought they were struggling alone.
It is a voluntary expression of generosity, not a requirement for salvation, spiritual maturity, or God's approval.
Biblically, giving is an act of worship when it is offered freely, sincerely, and for God's purposes.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
The New Testament also recognizes the legitimacy of supporting those engaged in gospel ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6).
But it should not be presented as a compulsory biblical tithe, nor should it replace responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those genuinely in need.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His word, love for others, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
For others, it may mean praying, sharing biblical resources, encouraging someone in need, or serving faithfully in their own church and community.
All of these can matter.

These products are not spiritual necessities, and buying them does not make anyone a more faithful Christian. They are simply practical resources and expressions of encouragement connected with the ministry.
We want people to have access to resources that encourage them to open their Bibles, examine what they believe, grow in discernment, and follow Christ faithfully.
We want you to know Christ.
To love His word.
To belong to a faithful local church.
To grow in prayer.
To resist the enemy's lies.
To walk in repentance.
To experience the transforming grace of God.
Because this is bigger than an article.
Bigger than a page.
Bigger than anything we could ever build.
This is about the eternal gospel of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that garden.
Imagine the silence after Adam and Eve sinned.
The terrible realization.
The shame.
The fear.
The hiding.
The broken fellowship.
The world that would never be the same.
Imagine the generations that followed, with all their suffering, violence, idolatry, death, and desperate longing for deliverance.
Then imagine a hill outside Jerusalem.
A cross.
A crown of thorns.
A Savior suffering for sinners.
And then an empty tomb.
A risen Lord.
A gospel proclaimed among the nations.
And finally, look toward the last pages of Revelation.
The ancient serpent judged.
The curse removed.
The throne of God and of the Lamb.
The river of the water of life.
The tree of life.
The servants of God seeing His face.
The same God who called to fallen humanity in the garden will dwell forever with His redeemed people.
The story that began with deception ends in the triumph of truth.
The story that introduced death ends with death abolished.
The story that revealed human shame ends with the redeemed dwelling in the presence of God.
And the One who makes that possible is Jesus Christ.
Not our goodness.
Not our religious performance.
Not our donations.
Not our ability to repair ourselves.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Son of God.
The Lamb who was slain.
The King who will reign forever.
The Savior whose grace is greater than the guilt of everyone who truly turns to Him.
So when the enemy reminds you of your past, remember the cross.
When temptation promises freedom through disobedience, remember Eden.
When suffering makes the future look hopeless, remember the empty tomb.
When evil appears to prosper, remember Revelation.
And when you wonder whether the final word over your life must be shame, look to the Savior who calls sinners out of hiding and into His marvelous light.
The serpent spoke a lie that brought humanity into ruin.
But Jesus Christ has spoken a greater word of redemption, sealed by His blood and vindicated by His resurrection.
The serpent's deception opened humanity's darkest chapter—but the Lamb's victory means darkness will never write the final sentence.
